items.prompt: Which sentence uses commas correctly in a list?

options.text: We bought, rice eggs chillies and bananas.
options.why: The comma should separate the items, not come after bought.

options.text: We bought rice, eggs, chillies and bananas.
We bought rice eggs, chillies, and, bananas.
options.why: There should be a comma after rice, and no comma after and.

options.text: We bought rice, eggs, chillies, and, bananas.
options.why: There should be no comma after and.

hints: Find the items in the list.
Commas go between the items. The last two items are joined by and.
Say the list aloud and pause where each comma is. Does it sound right?
items.explanation: In a list, commas separate the items, and the last two are joined with and: rice, eggs, chillies and bananas.

items.prompt: Where should the comma go? After lunch we played football.

options.text: after lunch
after we
options.why: We is part of the main clause, so it should not be separated from played.

options.text: after played
after football
options.why: The sentence ends after football, so it needs a full stop.

hints: The sentence starts with words that tell us when.
A comma usually follows a fronted adverbial, the phrase at the start that tells when, where or how.
Find the words that tell you when. Where do they end?
items.explanation: After lunch is a fronted adverbial telling us when, so a comma follows it: After lunch, we played football.

items.prompt: Which words could go in brackets? My cousin Raka who is ten plays the drums. Write them.
hints: Brackets hold extra information that the sentence could manage without.
Try reading the sentence and leaving out a group of words. Does it still make sense?
Read the sentence without three of its words. Which three can you take out?
items.explanation: Who is ten is extra information. The sentence still makes sense without it: My cousin Raka (who is ten) plays the drums.

options.text: Borobudur (a huge temple) in Central Java) is visited by many people.
options.why: There is one opening bracket but two closing brackets.

options.text: Borobudur a huge temple (in Central Java is visited by many people.)
options.why: The brackets should go around the extra information only.

options.text: (Borobudur) a huge temple in Central Java is visited by many people.
options.why: Borobudur is the main subject, so it should not be in brackets.

options.text: Borobudur (a huge temple in Central Java) is visited by many people.

hints: Brackets come in pairs, around extra information.
Read each sentence without the words in brackets. It should still make sense.
Check that each sentence has one opening bracket and one closing bracket.
items.explanation: The extra information a huge temple in Central Java sits inside one pair of brackets, and the sentence makes sense without it.

items.prompt: Why are brackets used in this sentence? The Komodo dragon (the largest lizard in the world) lives on a few islands in Indonesia.

options.text: to show that someone is speaking
to separate the items in a list
options.why: Commas separate items in a list.

options.text: to add extra information that the sentence could manage without
to show the most important idea
options.why: The words in brackets are extra, not the main idea.

hints: Read the sentence without the words in brackets.
Does the sentence still make sense? Then think about what the brackets add.
Ask: is the information in brackets needed, or is it a bonus fact?
items.explanation: Brackets add extra information. The sentence makes sense without the words inside them.

items.prompt: Choose 2 sentences that use commas correctly to mark extra information.

options.text: Mr Tan, our new neighbour, grows chillies.
The mango which, was very ripe fell from the tree.
options.why: The commas should go before which and after ripe.

options.text: The mango, which was very ripe, fell from the tree.
Mr Tan our new, neighbour grows chillies.
options.why: The commas should go around our new neighbour.

options.text: My bag, is under the desk.
options.why: There is no extra information here, so no comma is needed.

hints: Extra information needs a comma before it and a comma after it.
Find the extra information in each sentence, then check where the commas are.
Read each sentence without the words between the commas. Does it still make sense?
items.explanation: In the correct sentences, the extra information our new neighbour and which was very ripe has a comma before it and a comma after it.

items.prompt: Sort the sentences: commas used correctly or needs fixing.

items.text: Although it was late, we kept reading.
The cat, sat on the mat.
Rudi, who loves maths, won a prize.
We had rice, fish, and, fruit.
If you are cold put on, a jumper.

hints: Look at where each comma is and why it is there.
Commas go after an opening clause or adverbial, around extra information and between list items.
Read each sentence aloud and pause at each comma. Does the pause make sense?
items.explanation: The correct sentences use a comma after an opening clause or adverbial and around extra information. The others put commas in places that split words that belong together.

items.prompt: A comma is missing. Write the word that the comma should come after. Although the road was flooded the bus kept going.
hints: The sentence starts with a subordinate clause.
When a subordinate clause comes first, a comma goes at the end of it.
Find where the although part ends and the main clause begins.
items.explanation: Although the road was flooded is a subordinate clause at the start, so a comma comes after flooded.

items.prompt: Which sentence shows clearly that the children washed themselves, and then the dog went for a walk?

options.text: After the children had washed the dog went for a walk.
options.why: Without a comma, it sounds as if the children washed the dog.

options.text: After, the children had washed the dog went for a walk.
options.why: A comma after After does not make sense here.

options.text: After the children had washed, the dog went for a walk.
After the children, had washed the dog went for a walk.
options.why: The comma splits the children from what they did.

hints: Read each sentence aloud, pausing at each comma.
A comma can show where one idea ends and the next begins.
Ask in each sentence: who or what did the washing?
items.explanation: The comma after washed shows that the first idea ends there. Without it, readers may think the children washed the dog.

items.prompt: How many commas does this sentence need? On Saturday morning Bu Rina who is our school nurse bought rice and chillies.
hints: Look for an opening phrase and for extra information.
An opening phrase needs one comma. Extra information needs a comma on each side.
Start with On Saturday morning. Where does it end?
items.explanation: The sentence needs three commas: On Saturday morning, Bu Rina, who is our school nurse, bought rice and chillies.
